name: Cuisine classique
summary: The kitchen of the grand hotel as Auguste Escoffier set it down. A brigade of stations cooks a menu of courses from a fixed system of stocks and mother sauces, and serves each dish on its own plate. Le Guide culinaire of 1903 holds about 5,000 recipes of the system.

philosophy.core_thesis: Simplify Carême and make the kitchen a system: every dish comes from a small set of bases, cooked by a station that does one task.
design_principles: Keep a white stock, a brown stock and a fish fumet ready each day; every sauce starts from one of them.
Derive each sauce from one of five mother sauces: espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomato and hollandaise.
Split the kitchen into stations: the saucier, the rôtisseur, the poissonnier, the entremetier, the garde-manger and the pâtissier.
Serve à la russe: one course after another, each on a plate, in the order of the menu.
Cut the number of garnishes, so that the main ingredient is the subject of the plate.
Name a dish after its garnish or a patron: Rossini, Melba, Véronique, Jeannette.
Finish each sauce with butter off the heat for a gloss.
Use the same cut for each piece of a garnish: julienne, brunoise, tournée to 7 faces.
anti_patterns: A sauce thickened with bread or ground almonds
Every dish of a meal on the table at once
An edible architecture of sugar and pastry on the table
A garnish that hides the main ingredient
Raw fish, raw meat or undercooked vegetables
A sauce made to order without a stock

plating.composition: One main piece at the centre of the plate under a coat of sauce, with a garnish of turned vegetables or a croûton beside it.
plating.plate: A white porcelain plate of 260 to 280 mm with a gold or a monogrammed rim, or a silver platter for the guéridon.
plating.portion: A main piece of 150 to 200 g with 60 to 80 ml of sauce and two or three garnishes.
plating.height: The food stands 20 to 40 mm high; the sauce coats the piece and pools 3 to 5 mm deep at its foot.
rules: Put the main piece at the centre and coat it, or put the sauce beside it in a sauce boat.
Turn each root vegetable to seven faces and 5 cm long.
Glaze a roast or a sauced piece so that it shines under the lamps of the dining room.
Carve or finish a large piece at a guéridon at the table, then plate it in front of the guest.
Keep the rim of the plate clean; wipe it before the plate leaves the pass.

pantry.rule: Build on butter, cream and veal stock; add a luxury ingredient (truffle, foie gras or caviar) to the dish of honour.

technique.bases: A white veal stock, a brown veal stock, a fish fumet, a demi-glace reduced from espagnole, and a stock of court-bouillon for poaching.
technique.details: A turned vegetable, a croûton fried in butter, a sauce finished with butter, a slice of truffle on a white sauce.

flavour.profile: Rich, round and meaty: reduced stock, butter and cream, with the perfume of truffle, Madeira and tarragon.
flavour.balance: Umami and fat lead; a little acid from wine, lemon or vinegar lifts the emulsion sauces; sweet stays in the dessert.
flavour.fat: Butter and cream give 40 to 60 per cent of the energy of a sauced main dish.
flavour.seasoning: Salt and white pepper, a bouquet garni in the stock, and fines herbes at the end. No chilli and few spices.

palette.strategy: Use the white of the plate and the ivory of the cream sauces, the brown of the demi-glace and the black of truffle, with one bright garnish.

service.format: Service à la russe in a hotel dining room: the waiter brings each course on a plate or carves it at a guéridon.
service.courses: Seven to twelve courses at a dinner: hors d'oeuvre, soup, fish, entrée, roast, salad, vegetable, sweet and dessert.
service.tableware: White porcelain with a gold rim, a silver cloche and platter, crystal glasses for each wine and a white linen cloth.
service.setting: A grand hotel with electric light; a brigade of 30 to 80 cooks under a chef de cuisine and a maître d'hôtel in tails.

positive: white porcelain plate with gold rim

evidence.title: Le guide culinaire, 1903 (title page and text)
evidence.credit: Auguste Escoffier; scan by the Wellcome Library

emotion.target_response: The calm of a perfect order: a known dish, cooked exactly, served by a staff who know their roles.

use_cases: a period dinner scene in a grand hotel
a menu for a classic French restaurant
a food photograph of a classic sauced dish
avoid_when: the brief wants a light or vegetable-led plate
the brief wants a modern tasting menu
the brief is home or street food

modifiers.request: lighter, shorter, plated by the chef
modifiers.how: Drop the roux, reduce the stock without flour, cook the fish pink, and arrange each plate in the kitchen on a large white plate.
Add a pièce montée, serve many dishes at once on the table, and dress each dish with hâtelets and aspic.

sources.title: Kenneth James, Escoffier: The King of Chefs (2002)
